newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada markets give weak applause to budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada markets give weak applause to budget.

text.p: Canadian markets weakly applauded the government's fiscal 1997/98 budget on Wednesday, calling it prudent, but offering little support in the way of buying action on the morning after.

Economists said Finance Minister Martin pulled off a difficult balancing act by holding firmly to the government's deficit-fighting program, while offering only minor tax cuts and new spending in what is expected to be an election year.
"I believe Mr. Martin has successfully walked the tightrope balancing political and economic pressures," wrote Nesbitt Burns Chief Economist Sherry Cooper in her economic assessment of the budget.

However Canada's dollar eased in morning trade after the budget to C$1.3565 from pre-budget levels around C$1.3546, with most traders saying much of the good news had already been priced into the currency market.

"There was so much in the way of free pre-budget information being distributed," said Reid Farrill, corporate foreign exchange advisor at CIBC-Wood Gundy Inc. "We needed to have some interest to buy Canada in the overseas market and we just didn't get that."
Martin predicted the deficit for fiscal 1996/97 would be no more that C$19 billion, compared to a projected C$24.3 billion. The deficit is seen falling to C$17 billion in 1997/98.

CIBC-Wood Gundy Inc chief economist Jeffrey Rubin wrote in his budget reaction that the continued fiscal restraint will drop the amount of bonds issued by the government to less than C$8.0 billion from nearly C$40 billion in 1996/97.
"Having all but completed the term extension of its debt, the federal government should be presiding over progressively smaller bond auctions as supply constraints move up the curve," Rubin wrote.
Canadian bonds opened slightly weaker on Wednesday, pulled lower by a decline in U.S. Treasury prices, with Tuesday's federal budget having little impact on markets overnight.

"Most of the weakness we're seeing in Canada is pretty much coming from the U.S." said Arve Bendiksrud, a fixed-income analyst with TD Securities Inc. "When we got the budget it was more or less as expected. We anticipated very little immediate impact.
Canada's 30-year bond fell C$0.15 to C$113.90 to yield 6.851 percent.
The Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's largest stock market which had rallied on Tuesday ahead of the budget to post a record close, was flat at Wednesday's opening.
The TSE-300 index hovered around 6238.22, with nine million shares traded worth C$133.8 million. Advances outpaced declines 272 to 184.

Although financial sector investors were disappointed that Martin retained a special surtax on Canadian banks, most were satisfied that he did not impose new corporate, personal or excise tax increases.
"Steady as she goes," said Maison Placements Canada trader Joe Ismail. "I didn't expect too much of a reaction to the budget anyhow."

Ismail said there was little, if anything, in the fiscal 1997/98 budget to move Canadian equities. Instead, players were trading on bullion prices. "Gold bullion is firming up in the short term: that will keep a steady keel on the Canadian market."
((Paul Casciato, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8100 or email: paul.casciato@reuters.com))
